title: Sampling Theorem Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Signal Processing
Sampling Theorem
Nyquist Frequency
Aliasing
Signal Reconstruction
description: Sample a sine wave at an adjustable rate and rebuild it from the samples with ideal sinc interpolation, a zero-order hold or linear interpolation. Time plots and a spectrum with the Nyquist frequency marked show why a tone above half the sampling rate folds to a lower alias frequency.

educational.topic: The sampling theorem, aliasing and reconstruction
learningObjectives: State the sampling theorem and the meaning of the Nyquist rate and the Nyquist frequency
Predict the alias frequency of an under-sampled tone
Explain aliasing as the overlap of spectral copies created by sampling
Compare ideal sinc reconstruction with zero-order hold and linear interpolation

equations: alias frequency = |fmax - k fs|, k = round(fmax / fs)
x_r(t) = sum over n of x[n] sinc((t - n Ts) / Ts)
zero-order hold gain = |sinc(f / fs)|, linear interpolation gain = sinc^2(f / fs)
assumptions: The input is a single sine with zero phase, so fmax is the tone frequency
The ideal reconstruction is drawn from the closed-form result of the infinite sinc sum

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Predict, test and explain with linked time and frequency views
keyQuestions: What happens to the reconstructed signal as the sampling rate falls below twice the signal frequency?
Why is sampling at exactly twice the signal frequency not enough?
Why does a zero-order hold need a smoothing filter after it?
commonMisconceptions: Sampling at exactly twice the highest frequency always allows perfect reconstruction
Aliasing can be removed by filtering after sampling
An under-sampled tone simply disappears instead of appearing at another frequency
assessmentOpportunities: Predict the alias frequency for (fmax, fs) = (40, 50), (70, 50), (30, 50) and (100, 30) Hz and check each
Explain the line heights in the spectrum for the zero-order hold
